The other three are all supported: on 1st June actual progress (about 22 per cent) is well below expected (about 50 per cent), so A is true; the actual line climbs from about 43 per cent to 100 per cent between Aug and 1st Sept, far steeper than any earlier month, so B is true; and the actual line reaches 100 per cent just before the 1st September gridline while the expected line reaches it only at that gridline, so C is true. items.value: 120 ways
items.reasoning: The three blocks are of different heights (first, second and third place), so they are distinguishable and the order of colours matters. The tallest block can take any of the 6 colours, the middle block any of the remaining 5, and the shortest any of the remaining 4, giving 6 x 5 x 4 = 120 arrangements. This is the permutation 6P3; the combination C(6,3) = 20 would be the answer only if the blocks were interchangeable, which they are not.

items.value: The population growth rate decreased between 1990 and 2010, because the gap between the birthrate and the death rate narrowed
items.reasoning: The rate of population growth is the gap between the birthrate and the death rate. By 1990 the death rate has already completed most of its fall (the graph shows it flattening to about 7 by 2000), whereas the birthrate is still falling through the 1980s and 1990s and only eases off to about 18 around 2000. So between 1990 and 2010 the birthrate drops appreciably while the death rate barely moves, which narrows the gap: from roughly 13 per thousand in 1990 to about 11 per thousand (18 minus 7) from 2000 onwards. A narrowing gap means a falling growth rate. Note that a falling growth rate does not mean a falling population: with births still exceeding deaths by about 11 per thousand, the population is still growing, only more slowly.

items.value: Only statements 2 and 4 follow: both the growth rate and the birthrate flatten after 2005, while the population itself has not stabilized and the death rate fell far more than 10 per cent in the first decade
items.reasoning: Taking 1970 as the base, 35 years later is 2005. Statement 4 is correct: the birthrate curve runs almost flat at about 18 from around 2000 to 2010. Statement 2 is correct for the same reason: with the birthrate flat at about 18 and the death rate flat at about 7, their difference (the growth rate) is a constant 11 per thousand after 2005. Statement 1 is wrong and is the classic trap here: a stable growth rate is not a stable population. Births still exceed deaths by 11 per thousand, so the population is still rising steadily. Statement 3 is wrong: in the first ten years the death rate falls from about 25 to roughly 15-17, a fall of well over 10 per cent (indeed of the order of 30-40 per cent), so a 10 per cent fall understates it badly. Only 2 and 4 survive, which is option D.

items.value: The slopes are the same in both figures: the two graphs plot identical data and differ only in where the vertical axis begins, so only the visual impression changes
items.reasoning: Both figures plot the same five points (20, 25, 30, 35, 40 for 2013 to 2017). Because the values are identical in the two figures, option A is false; because the range is 40 minus 20 = 20 in both, option B is false; and because earnings rise by 5 per year in both, the rate of increase is identical and option D is false. That leaves C, which is also true on its own terms: the slope of the data, dE/dY, is 5 per year in each figure. Fig. A merely looks steeper because its vertical axis starts at 20 instead of 0, which stretches the same rise over more of the page. The whole point of the item is that a truncated axis changes appearance without changing any quantity.

items.value: A straight bar with a filled square head and two bent legs
items.reasoning: Across all eight filled cells the bar and the head are locked together in fixed pairs: a concave-up curve always carries a filled circle, a straight bar always carries a filled square, and an arch always carries an open triangle. The three bar-and-head types and the three leg types each appear exactly once per row and once per column, so the grid is a pair of Latin squares. Row 3 already has the arch and the concave-up curve, and column 3 already has the arch and the concave-up curve, so the missing cell must be the straight bar, and therefore the filled square head. Row 3 already has three-leg and four-leg forms, and column 3 already has four-leg and three-leg forms, so the missing cell must have two bent legs. Straight bar, filled square, two bent legs is option A. B fails because a circle head cannot sit on a straight bar, C fails on both head and legs, and D additionally puts the head at the wrong end.

items.value: 2000 pieces, where revenue of Rs 7,00,000 exactly equals the production cost of Rs 7 lakh
items.reasoning: From Fig. A the cost of production is 5 lakh plus 1 lakh for every 1000 pieces, so 1000 pieces cost 6 lakh, 2000 cost 7 lakh and 3000 cost 8 lakh. From Fig. B the selling price per piece is Rs 400 at 1000 pieces, Rs 350 at 2000 and Rs 300 at 3000. Revenue is therefore 1000 x 400 = Rs 4,00,000 against a cost of Rs 6,00,000 (a loss of two lakh); 2000 x 350 = Rs 7,00,000 against a cost of Rs 7,00,000 (exactly break-even); and 3000 x 300 = Rs 9,00,000 against a cost of Rs 8,00,000 (a profit of one lakh). Since break-even is not a loss, 2000 pieces is the smallest quantity at which a loss is avoided. Note that the falling price means revenue does not rise in proportion to output, which is why the answer is not simply the largest option.

items.value: 10 children
items.reasoning: The lift holds 18 adults or 30 children, so 18 adults occupy exactly the same capacity as 30 children, which means 6 adults are equivalent to 10 children. With 12 adults already aboard, the space of 18 minus 12 = 6 adults is left, and that space takes 10 children. Equivalently, 12 adults use two-thirds of the capacity, and the remaining one-third of 30 is 10.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 follow; statement 2 is false because country A's dependency ratio will be higher than country B's, not lower
items.reasoning: Dependency ratio is the under-15 and over-64 groups taken together, divided by the 15-64 working-age group. In country B the working-age curve climbs steadily throughout while the under-15 group merely plateaus and the elderly group rises slowly, so over the last twenty-five years the ratio has fallen: statement 1 is correct. Statement 3 is correct for the same reason: over the next two decades B's working-age line keeps rising towards 1.1 million while A's has already peaked around 2010 and is falling, so the workforce share of total population rises in B and falls in A. Statement 2 is the one to reject. By 2050 country A has about 0.22 under-15 plus 0.33 elderly against a workforce of about 0.88, a ratio near 0.63, whereas country B has about 0.28 plus 0.27 against a workforce of about 1.1, a ratio near 0.50. A is ageing (its elderly curve overtakes its under-15 curve around 2030) so its dependency ratio will be higher than B's, the opposite of what statement 2 claims.

items.value: Lakshmi's brother is the best player
items.reasoning: The two sibling pairs are Lakshmi with her brother, and her daughter with her son. Clue (i) puts the brother and the daughter on opposite sides, so the two possible line-ups are brother partnered with the son against daughter and Lakshmi, or brother partnered with Lakshmi against daughter and son. In the first line-up the son is diagonally opposite the daughter, so by clue (ii) the daughter is the worst player's sibling, which makes the son the worst player; by clue (iii) the best player is on the son's side, and it cannot be the son, so it is the brother. In the second line-up the son is diagonally opposite the brother, so the brother is the worst player's sibling, which makes Lakshmi the worst player; the best player is then on Lakshmi's side and is not Lakshmi, so again it is the brother. Both admissible arrangements give the same answer, so the brother is the best player.

items.value: An anti-inflationary stance: repeated increases in the repo and reverse repo rates are the standard tool for tightening money and curbing inflation
items.reasoning: The graph shows the repo rate climbing from 5.50 to 7.50 per cent and the reverse repo from 4.00 to 6.50 per cent in nine steps over a year. Raising the policy rates makes borrowing from the central bank costlier and idle funds parked with it more rewarding, which contracts credit and drains liquidity from the system, the classic response to inflationary pressure. Option B is the exact opposite of the effect of a rate rise. Option A is not a policy-rate objective, and although higher rates may incidentally make deposits more attractive, encouraging savings is a by-product rather than the reason a central bank tightens repeatedly, so C is not the most likely reason. The fact that the CRR is held flat at 6.00 throughout while only the rates are raised is consistent with a price-directed tightening rather than a liquidity injection.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 follow; statement 2 fails because of the word always
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is supported as a general tendency: the nine states with per capita income below 600 dollars average a tele-density of about 41, while the nine above 700 dollars average about 85. The word generally accommodates the two outliers, States 4 and 8, which have very low tele-density. Statement 2 is false as stated: State 3 has one of the highest growth rates at 10.83 per cent yet the lowest per capita income at 254 dollars, while State 14 grows at only 5.46 per cent on a per capita income of 864 dollars, so a high growth rate does not always ensure a high per capita income. Statement 3 is true and is proved by the same kind of case in reverse: State 4 grows at 9.78 per cent with a tele-density of only 5.94, and State 14 grows slowly at 5.46 per cent with a tele-density of 97.9. Note that statements 2 and 3 differ mainly in strength, always ensures against does not necessarily ensure, and it is that difference that separates them.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid: the table shows an association only, and both assumptions overstate it into a necessary condition
items.reasoning: The table records per capita income, GDP growth and tele-density for one year; it shows a broad correlation but says nothing about causation, about investment in telecom infrastructure, or about what sustains prosperity over time, so assumption 1 is not something the data supports. Assumption 2 is contradicted by the table itself: State 4 grows at 9.78 per cent with a tele-density of just 5.94 and State 8 grows at 5.92 per cent with a tele-density of 6, so a very high tele-density cannot be the most essential condition for economic growth. Both assumptions convert a loose statistical association into an absolute requirement, using cannot be sustained without and most essential condition, which the single-year data cannot bear.

items.value: Only statement 1 follows: direct taxes rose as a share of gross tax revenue while indirect taxes fell; nothing about manufacturing growth can be read off the excise share
items.reasoning: Direct taxes are corporate tax and personal income tax. Corporate tax rises from about 9 to about 42 per cent of gross tax revenue and personal income tax from about 10 to about 19, so together they climb from roughly 19 to roughly 61. Indirect taxes are excise, customs and service tax, which move from about 42.5, 36 and 0 to about 19.5, 17.5 and 10.5, that is from roughly 78.5 down to roughly 47.5. Statement 1 is therefore correct. Statement 2 is not: the graph plots each tax only as a percentage of gross tax revenue, so a falling excise share is entirely consistent with excise collections and manufacturing output both growing in absolute terms, merely more slowly than corporate tax receipts. A share cannot be read as a level, and manufacturing growth is not plotted at all.

items.value: None of the three statements must be true; x - y = 8 permits both x and y to be negative, both positive, or either sign
items.reasoning: Statement 1 fails at x = 8, y = 0, or at x = 0, y = -8, where the difference is 8 but the numbers are not both positive. Statement 2 fails at x = 10, y = 2, where x is positive and y is positive as well while x - y is still 8. Statement 3 fails because if x is negative then y = x - 8 is less than -8, so y is necessarily negative, never positive; the statement asserts precisely the wrong sign. Since none of the three must hold, the answer is the blanket denial. The item is printed with an asymmetry, three numbered statements but options (a) to (c) referring only to statements 1 and 2, and it is answered here as printed; the asymmetry does not affect the outcome, because every statement is false and only option (d) covers that case.

items.value: The environmental cost of industrially farmed meat is unsustainable
items.reasoning: The passage builds a case against factory farming and closes with its only quantified evidence, the water figures: 15000 litres per kilogram of meat against 3400 for rice, 3300 for eggs and 255 for potatoes. That comparison is what turns the description into an argument, and option D states it as a conclusion the passage supports. Option A contradicts the passage outright. Option B introduces laws against cruelty, which the passage never mentions; describing conditions as cruel is not the same as alleging a legal violation. Option C is the runner-up and is the one to weigh: the passage does present industrial meat production as undesirable, so its first half is fair, but the passage nowhere calls for the practice to be stopped immediately, and a message question asks what the passage conveys rather than what the reader would prescribe. For C to win, the item would have to treat the accumulated criticism as an implicit demand for abolition; if the setter read the passage as chiefly about cruelty and pandemics rather than about resource use, C becomes defensible.

items.value: Recognized wildlife corridors between protected areas are an essential part of conservation
items.reasoning: The passage ends by stating the point directly: prey and tigers can only disperse if there are recognized corridors of land between protected areas to allow unmolested passage. Everything before it sets that up, the reserves described as islands of habitat in a sea of humanity and the tiger that walked 250 miles because it needed range. Option A is more pessimistic than the passage, which offers corridors as a remedy rather than declaring the conflict unresolvable. Option C misreads the remedy: the passage asks for connections between existing protected areas, not for more of them. Option D raises professional management, which the passage never discusses.

items.value: Neither assumption is valid: the passage neither claims relocation usually fails nor says anything about legislation or failed conservation efforts
items.reasoning: Assumption 2 is clearly invalid: the passage never mentions legislation, and it attributes tigers living outside reserves to their wide ranging behaviour and to fragmented habitat, not to a failure of conservation efforts. Assumption 1 is the runner-up and needs the judgement call. The passage reports a single relocated tiger that walked home, and it uses that anecdote to introduce a crisis it then defines explicitly as habitat fragmentation and the absence of corridors, not as the unreliability of relocation. One instance cannot support the frequency claim not often successful, so the author need not be assuming it. For option A to win, the setter would have to read the anecdote as being offered as evidence that relocation itself does not work, in which case the author would indeed be presupposing that relocations commonly fail; that reading is available, which is why this is marked MED rather than HIGH.
